overview: The Thousand Pillar Temple, officially the Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple and locally called 'Veyyi Stambala Gudi', is a star-shaped Trikutalayam (triple-shrine complex) at the base of Hanamakonda Hill in Hanamakonda, Telangana. Built in 1163 CE by the Kakatiya king Rudra Deva, it took roughly 72 years to complete and is one of the earliest surviving masterpieces of Kakatiya art, architecture and sculpture. The complex, dedicated to Lord Shiva (Rudreshwara, east), Lord Vishnu (south) and Surya Deva (west), features close to 1,000 intricately carved pillars, a monolithic dolerite Nandi, perforated stone screens, rock-cut elephants and a restored Kalyana Mandapam. Centrally protected by the Archaeological Survey of India since 2001, it is on India's UNESCO tentative World Heritage list as part of 'The Glorious Kakatiya Temples and Gateways'. It is geographically and administratively distinct from the Ramappa Temple (UNESCO World Heritage Site 2021) at Palampet in Mulugu District, ~75 km away.
summary: The Thousand Pillar Temple (Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple) is a 1163 CE Kakatiya Trikutalayam at Hanamakonda, Warangal, Telangana, dedicated to Shiva (Rudreshwara), Vishnu and Surya. Built by Kakatiya king Rudra Deva in late Chalukyan / early Kakatiya (Vesara) style using dolerite and granite, it is famed for its ~1,000 carved pillars, monolithic Nandi, and the earthquake-resistant 'sandbox' foundation. It is NOT a UNESCO World Heritage Site — only the Ramappa Temple (Palampet, ~75 km away) carries that designation since 2021. The Thousand Pillar is on UNESCO's tentative list alongside Warangal Fort and Kakatiya Kala Thoranam, and is centrally protected by the ASI.

history.content: The temple was built in 1163 CE under the patronage of the Kakatiya king Rudra Deva (Rudradeva I), and construction is generally reported to have taken about 72 years (sources commonly cite c. 1175–1324 CE as the broader build/expansion window). It is named after its builder-king as Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple, with the presiding Shiva deity known as Rudreshwara. Successive Kakatiya rulers — Ganapati Deva, Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra — patronised and expanded the complex over the 12th–14th centuries. Per popular temple lore, King Rudra Deva had a divine vision in which Lord Shiva directed him to build a temple with a thousand pillars, each symbolically representing a lingam (this account is recorded in popular/tourism sources rather than a verifiable primary religious text).
founders: Subsequent Kakatiya patrons: Ganapati Deva, Rudrama Devi, Prataparudra

history.content: In the 14th century the temple complex — particularly the Kalyana Mandapam — suffered significant damage during the Deccan invasions of the Delhi Sultanate's Tughlaq dynasty; the core shrines survived due to their massive stone foundations and the Kakatiya 'sandbox' foundation technique. In the early 20th century, Mir Osman Ali Khan, the seventh Nizam of Hyderabad, contributed a grant (~₹1 lakh) toward reconstruction. The temple was declared a protected monument by the Archaeological Survey of India in 2001 and renovated by the Government of India in 2004. It is on India's UNESCO World Heritage tentative list under 'The Glorious Kakatiya Temples and Gateways' (alongside Warangal Fort and Kakatiya Kala Thoranam). In the 2020s, the ASI completed a long-running restoration of the fallen Kalyana Mandapam, rebuilding it stone-by-stone using the original Kakatiya 'sandbox' foundation technique. ASI has reportedly spent ~₹9.90 crore on restoration. The temple is NOT (and has never been) inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site — only the Ramappa Temple at Palampet (~75 km away) carries that designation (inscribed 25 July 2021, UNESCO ref 1570).

sthala_puranam: According to popular temple legend, King Rudra Deva had a divine vision in which Lord Shiva directed him to build a temple with a thousand pillars, each symbolically representing a lingam. The king is said to have undertaken the construction in fulfilment of this divine command. (This account is recorded in popular/tourism sources rather than a verifiable primary religious text and should be treated as traditional temple lore.)
religious_significance: The temple holds importance as a Trikutalayam housing the grouping of Shiva, Vishnu and Surya (Surya replacing Brahma in this particular grouping) within one interconnected complex — an arrangement considered relatively distinctive among South Indian temples. Trimurti Puja performed here is regarded as symbolic of unified worship of the three deities.
spiritual_significance: Devotees traditionally believe the temple's orientation was deliberately designed so that the first rays of the morning sun fall directly upon the Shiva lingam in the sanctum, reflecting the Kakatiya rulers' devotion to Shiva and their astronomical/architectural planning. The temple is popularly regarded as a symbol of the artistic and spiritual zenith of Kakatiya civilisation in Telangana.
healing_beliefs: Devotees believe the temple's serene environment and sacred vibrations promote mental peace and spiritual healing.
Pilgrimage associated with general welfare and relief from planetary afflictions through worship of the Shiva-Vishnu-Surya triad.
miracles_and_devotee_experiences: The core shrines survived 14th-century Tughlaq invasions despite damage to the Kalyana Mandapam, widely attributed to the Kakatiya 'sandbox' foundation technique (sand-filled pit absorbing seismic shocks).
The temple has remained standing through multiple earthquakes over the centuries, again attributed to advanced Kakatiya engineering.
Devotees report a sense of divine energy and tranquility; the temple's floating-brick-free (stone) construction and intricate carvings are considered feats of medieval engineering.
architecture: The temple reflects late Chalukyan and early Kakatiya architectural traditions (broadly Vesara style), built primarily of dolerite/black basalt and granite. It is a 'Trikutalayam' — a star-shaped, triple-shrine complex where the Shiva shrine faces east and the Vishnu and Surya shrines face south and west, all connected to a central mandapam so that no pillar obstructs the view of any deity. It features close to 1,000 intricately carved stone pillars, a ~6-foot monolithic Nandi carved from a single block of black basalt/dolerite facing the Shiva shrine, a restored Kalyana Mandapam (dance/marriage hall, ASI-restored in the 2020s using the original 'sandbox' foundation technique), the natya mandapam (dance hall) at the front, rock-cut elephant sculptures, perforated stone screens, finely carved doorways, and inscriptions. The structure is elevated on a 1-metre platform that slopes gently toward Hanamakonda Hill.

introduction.en: The Thousand Pillar Temple, officially the Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple and locally called Veyyi Stambala Gudi, is a 1163 CE Kakatiya Trikutalayam at the base of Hanamakonda Hill in Hanamakonda, Telangana. A triple-shrine complex, it houses Shiva as Rudreshwara, Vishnu and Surya connected by a central mandapam of close to a thousand carved pillars, with a monolithic Nandi and a restored Kalyana Mandapam. Built by Kakatiya king Rudra Deva, it is now an ASI-protected monument on India's UNESCO tentative list. It is a separate monument from the Ramappa Temple UNESCO site at Palampet, about 75 kilometres away.

history.en: Built in 1163 CE by Kakatiya king Rudra Deva, with construction spanning about 72 years, the Thousand Pillar Temple was expanded by his successors Ganapati Deva, Rudrama Devi and Prataparudra. In the 14th century Tughlaq invasions damaged the Kalyana Mandapam, though the core shrines survived. The seventh Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan, granted funds for reconstruction in the early twentieth century. The ASI declared it a protected monument in 2001, renovated it in 2004, and recently completed a stone-by-stone restoration of the Kalyana Mandapam using the original sandbox foundation technique, spending about 9.9 crore rupees. It is on UNESCO's tentative list, not a World Heritage Site.

travel_guide.en: The Thousand Pillar Temple is on the Hyderabad-Warangal Highway, NH-163, in Brahmanawada, Hanamakonda, about 150 kilometres from Hyderabad, roughly a three hour drive. The nearest railway stations are Warangal, about five to six kilometres away, and Kazipet Junction, about seven to ten kilometres. The nearest airport is Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad, 150 to 170 kilometres away. Visiting hours are generally 6:00 AM to 8:00 PM, though some sources cite 5:00 AM to 9:00 PM. October to March is the best season.

faq.question: Where is the Thousand Pillar Temple located?
faq.answer: It is located at the base of Hanamakonda Hill in Hanamakonda (Hanamkonda), part of the Warangal tri-city area in Telangana, India, on the Hyderabad–Warangal Highway (NH-163), Brahmanawada. Pincode 506011.

faq.question: Who built the Thousand Pillar Temple, and when?
faq.answer: It was built in 1163 CE by the Kakatiya king Rudra Deva (Rudradeva I); construction is generally reported to have taken about 72 years (c. 1175–1324 CE build/expansion window per multiple sources).

faq.question: Which deities are worshipped at the temple?
faq.answer: It is a Trikutalayam dedicated to Lord Shiva (Rudreshwara, east-facing), Lord Vishnu (south-facing) and Surya Deva (Sun God, west-facing).

faq.question: What is the temple's other/official name?
faq.answer: It is officially the Sri Rudreshwara Swamy Temple and is locally called 'Veyyi Stambala Gudi' (Thousand Pillar Temple in Telugu).

faq.question: What are the temple's visiting hours?
faq.answer: Most sources report approximately 6:00 AM to 8:00 PM daily (e.g. Tripadvisor, Inheritage, Outlook Traveller); a few sources cite 5:00 AM to 9:00 PM with extended hours during festivals. Confirm current timings locally before visiting.

faq.question: Is there an entry fee?
faq.answer: Most sources indicate free general entry; a few travel blogs mention a nominal fee (~₹15 Indian / ~₹200 foreign), possibly for adjoining ASI facilities. Unresolved from official sources — confirm on-site.

faq.question: Who currently manages/maintains the temple?
faq.answer: It is a centrally protected monument under the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI), with religious administration / day-to-day worship coordinated through Telangana state authorities (Endowments Department).

faq.question: Is the Thousand Pillar Temple a UNESCO World Heritage Site?
faq.answer: No — it is on India's UNESCO tentative list (as part of 'The Glorious Kakatiya Temples and Gateways') but is not yet inscribed as a World Heritage Site. The nearby Ramappa Temple at Palampet, Mulugu district (~75 km away) was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site on 25 July 2021 (UNESCO reference 1570). They are two separate monuments.

faq.question: Is the Thousand Pillar Temple the same as the Ramappa Temple?
faq.answer: No. They are two distinct Kakatiya monuments: the Thousand Pillar Temple is in Hanamakonda, Hanamakonda District, Telangana, and is an ASI-protected monument on the UNESCO tentative list. The Ramappa Temple is in Palampet, Mulugu District, Telangana (~75 km from Hanamakonda), and is the actual UNESCO World Heritage Site (inscribed 2021). Both share Kakatiya architectural style but differ in date (1163 CE vs 1213 CE), layout, presiding deity grouping, and protection status.

faq.question: What is the best time of year to visit?
faq.answer: October to March (cooler, ~15–25°C). Maha Shivaratri (Feb/Mar) and Karthika Pournami are the most festive times but also the most crowded.

faq.question: How do I reach the temple from Hyderabad?
faq.answer: By road ~150 km (~3 hours) via NH-163; by rail via Warangal Railway Station (~5–6 km) or Kazipet Junction (~7–10 km); by air via Rajiv Gandhi International Airport, Hyderabad (~150–170 km), then onward road transport.

faq.question: Can people of all faiths visit?
faq.answer: Yes — multiple sources note the temple is open to visitors of all faiths, being both an active place of worship and a protected heritage/tourist site.

faq.question: Are photography and videography allowed?
faq.answer: Mobile photography is generally allowed in most areas; videography or professional photography may require permission and could involve a nominal charge in certain areas — confirm on-site with ASI/temple staff.
